data.content_ref: inline:The target nominates sky view factor (SVF) as the single mechanism that best explains why the nocturnal UHI gap is larger in some cities than in others, but under the very conditions the problem fixes (clear, calm night), SVF is not the dominant cross-city modulator. On a clear, calm night the nocturnal UHI is overwhelmingly governed by the release of heat stored in urban materials during the previous day: dense impervious surfaces with high thermal admittance retain more daytime heat and release it slowly after sunset, keeping the city warmer. SVF sets the maximum possible radiative cooling rate, but once calm conditions suppress turbulent removal and longwave loss is established, the residual warmth is supplied by stored heat. Consequently the cross-city variance in the gap is driven primarily by differences in thermal storage/admittance and anthropogenic heat release (asphalt, concrete, building mass, energy use), not by geometry alone. The countercondition about wide streets/low density concedes that population and city size can decouple from SVF, yet the claim still elevates SVF over stored heat. Naming 'thermal mass' or 'sensible heat' in passing does not establish that storage release is the best single explanation; the target's thesis is that SVF is the governing mechanism, which inverts the dominant cause. A low-SVF city built on low-admittance dry sandy soil with little impervious cover would have a small nocturnal gap, while a high-SVF but high-admittance city full of asphalt and concrete would have a large gap.
